request_payload.input: We are comparing two English natural-language-inference classifiers. We want to know which one better tracks who did what to whom when deciding whether a hypothesis follows from a premise, including cases where the two sentences use almost the same words. Recommend a public evaluation resource and scoring plan, and state what conclusion it would justify.
request_payload.instructions: Answer the research question from existing knowledge. Aim for 180–240 words and do not exceed 300 words. Do not browse or use external tools. Do not ask a follow-up question.

output_text:
Use the HANS (Heuristic Analysis for NLI Systems) dataset, a public benchmark released by McCoy, Pavlick, and Linzen (2019) and available through the GLUE diagnostic suite. HANS contains premise-hypothesis pairs with almost identical vocabulary but altered argument structure—subject-object swaps, active/passive alternations, and constituent reorderings—so that models relying on lexical overlap will wrongly predict entailment. The non-entailed examples are the key diagnostic for role tracking.

Scoring plan: Run both classifiers on HANS and compute overall accuracy. More importantly, isolate the high-overlap, role-sensitive subset where the hypothesis reorders the premise’s arguments but is not entailed. For each system, calculate accuracy on this subset and the false-entailment rate—the proportion of non-entailed pairs labeled entailment. Compare the two classifiers with a paired test such as McNemar’s test or bootstrap confidence intervals.

Conclusion: If one classifier achieves significantly higher accuracy on these near-duplicate-word, role-reversed pairs and a lower false-entailment rate, the evaluation justifies the conclusion that it better tracks who did what to whom rather than defaulting to lexical overlap. If the difference is not statistically significant, HANS does not warrant claiming superiority on this specific capability.
